d.title: Who decides, and how many times
d.caption: **The whole difference is control flow.** Baseline RAG runs the same way whatever the question and retrieves exactly once; agentic RAG makes retrieval a decision the model takes, repeatedly. **The capability worth naming first is not retrieving at all** — “hallo” and “what did I just ask” need no corpus, and a fixed pipeline retrieves for both, wasting a call and putting irrelevant chunks where they can mislead. And the clause interviewers react to is the cap: a corpus that cannot answer will not start being able to on the fourth attempt.

d.title: The one fact the whole reranking answer rests on
d.caption: **A cross-encoder cannot be precomputed, because the query–document pair does not exist until the query arrives.** Everything else follows: why it is accurate (full attention across the pair), why it cannot run over millions, and why the two-stage design exists at all. **And when the interviewer takes it away, lead with rank fusion** — it needs no model, it is immune to cosine and BM25 scores being incomparable, and it is what most production systems actually use.

d.title: The latency budget, and why the index is not the answer
d.caption: **The question invites a list of index tricks and the honest reply is that generation dominates.** Retrieval is 50–150 ms of a multi-second answer, so tuning the index optimises a few per cent — saying that, then giving the retrieval answers anyway, is what shows you would measure before tuning. **And the follow-up to pre-empt:** how do you know the ANN recall is good enough? You measure recall@k against exact search on a sample and tune `ef_search` until it is acceptable. An index tuned by feel has an unknown recall.

d.title: Index a text representation, return the original
d.caption: **One idea covers both tables and images**, and stating it as one idea rather than two shows the design rather than the recipe. **The strongest move on this question is the last node:** an aggregation like “total revenue in Q3” is a query rather than a lookup, and models do arithmetic over retrieved tables badly — so load it and give the agent a query tool instead of retrieving it at all.

d.title: Metrics per layer, not a flat list
d.caption: **A system that retrieves, decides and answers fails in three different ways**, so naming them by layer is the structure that lands. **Lead with groundedness:** it catches the failure that matters most and is invisible to every other metric — a fluent answer the context does not support. And tool-trajectory accuracy is the agentic metric *and* the model-upgrade regression test, because it moves more than anything else when the model changes.

d.title: Six steps, and step two is the one that impresses
d.caption: **Ask when it started before asking what caused it**, because a cliff and a slope have disjoint cause lists — that single question halves the search space. Most people begin at step four, which is why beginning earlier reads as experience. **And the most-forgotten cause is a silently updated model version:** the provider moved a pointer alias, your prompt was tuned for the old behaviour, and nothing in your repository changed.

d.title: Three questions before any multi-agent design
d.caption: **The first bounds the whole system**, and it is the question the ADK and MCP material keeps returning to: assume the model does exactly the wrong thing, and see what happens. **The second is the one that earns credit for restraint** — the question invites you to design something elaborate, and multi-agent adds routing failures, context loss between agents and a much harder debugging story. If one agent with six tools works, that is the system.

d.title: 250 GiB of cache for 14 GiB of weights
d.caption: **That is the number that makes the point.** The cache scales linearly in context length *and* batch size, which is why long context and high concurrency are the same problem — and why a 7B model's cache dwarfs its weights at any realistic concurrency. **GQA is the default answer** (4×, little quality loss, which is why recent models ship with it); MQA is 32× at a real quality cost; quantisation multiplies with either. And the non-memory answer is to send less context, since sequence length is the term everything is multiplied by.

d.title: Watch the banana column
d.caption: **0.0003 at T=1.0 and 0.0110 at T=2.0 — a 37-fold rise in the chance of nonsense.** That is what “raising temperature increases creativity” actually means: it raises the probability of every unlikely token, and the model cannot distinguish the creative ones from the wrong ones. **And the interaction people miss:** the same top_p=0.9 kept 2 tokens at T=1.0 and 4 at T=2.0, because temperature reshapes the distribution that top_p then measures. Tune one and leave the other.

d.title: Five mitigations, and the one that is usually the real answer
d.caption: **Catastrophic forgetting is over-training on a narrow task** — gradient updates overwrite the weights that encoded the old capabilities, and the loss is invisible unless you measure the general capability during the run. **LoRA is the first answer because the base weights are literally unchanged**, which also lets you swap or disable the adapter. But the last row is the one that most often applies: most cases reaching for fine-tuning are retrieval or prompting problems, and fine-tuning teaches form while RAG supplies facts.

d.title: The signal that separates operators from readers
d.caption: **A user id is invaluable on a span and fatal as a Prometheus label**, because every distinct label value creates a new time series and a million users is a million series. That one distinction is the strongest thing to say on the observability question. **And the principle underneath the whole answer:** alert on symptoms, diagnose with causes — which is what keeps an alert set from growing into hundreds of rules nobody trusts.

d.title: Threads for waiting, processes for computing
d.caption: **Threads were slower than doing it sequentially** — 0.68× — because only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time, so nothing overlaps and the GIL contention is pure added overhead. On IO the same pool gave 3.97× on four workers, because `sleep`, a socket read and a disk read all release the GIL. **For the 50k-document pipeline that maps directly:** processes for parsing (CPU-bound), async for the embedding calls (IO-bound at high concurrency), and threads mainly for wrapping a blocking library.

d.title: Five places a guardrail sits, and four layers of RBAC
d.caption: **A guardrail is a control that does not depend on the model cooperating** — which is why a system-prompt rule is never a security property, since the whole premise of prompt injection is that the model can be talked out of it. **And for RBAC the same logic gives four layers**, of which only the last cannot be talked past: identity from the session rather than a tool parameter, the tool list filtered by role so there is no declaration to call, the retrieval query scoped, and row-level security in the database.

d.title: Three solutions, in the order to present them
d.caption: **Do not open with the two-pointer version** — jumping to the trick reads as memorised, and the progression is what an easy-to-medium question is actually assessing. Say the brute force, notice the repeated scans, precompute the maxima, then notice you only need the *smaller* of the two maxima and the space collapses. **The invariant to say out loud:** water above a bar is `min(tallest left, tallest right) - height`, and when `h[lo] < h[hi]` you already know something at least as tall sits on the right, so the left maximum alone decides it.

d.title: Four problems, not one acronym
d.caption: **The weak answer expands the acronym; the strong one names the problems, because there are four and they are different.** The hallucination row carries the honest caveat worth saying aloud: RAG reduces invention because the model is summarising rather than recalling, and it does **not** stop the model inventing when retrieval returns nothing. **And the comparison they are listening for:** fine-tuning teaches form and behaviour, RAG supplies facts — which complaint you have decides which tool you reach for.

d.title: The deciding question, not the list
d.caption: **What is the smallest unit that can answer a question on its own?** Smaller than that cannot answer; much larger dilutes the embedding, because an embedding is one vector for everything in the chunk. **And the signal worth as much as the list: knowing when to stop.** Look at retrieved chunks for failing questions — cut mid-argument means the splitter is wrong, relevant-but-still-wrong means chunking is not the problem and further tuning is wasted effort.

d.title: Classify the PDF before parsing it
d.caption: **Step one is the one people skip, and it decides everything downstream:** OCR on a digital PDF is slow and lossy, and text extraction on a scan returns nothing at all. **Reading order is what plain extraction loses** — a two-column paper extracted naively interleaves the columns into nonsense, which is silent and corrupts every multi-column page. And OCR quality bounds everything after it, so check it on a sample before building the rest.

d.caption: **Pull fifty failing questions and ask whether the right chunk was in the context.** If it was not, the work is retrieval; if it was there and the answer was still wrong, adding retrieval techniques costs latency and changes nothing. **Saying this unprompted is the strongest move on the question**, because it invites a list and rewards a procedure. And the ordering underneath: hybrid search is the highest-value single change, and without recall@k on a golden set every item becomes an opinion.

d.title: Name the failure each technique fixes

d.title: 99.11% accuracy, and it caught nothing
d.caption: **The degenerate model is the fastest way to explain why the three metrics exist**, and it is a measurement rather than a claim. Then the threshold rows show the trade on *the same model*: precision 0.03 with recall 0.98, against precision 0.61 with recall 0.25. **And the last two rows are the detail that marks experience** — ROC-AUC reads 0.95 because it is dominated by the vast negative class, while average precision reads 0.36 against a random baseline of 0.0089. On imbalanced problems, report PR-AUC.

d.title: Who controls the flow
d.caption: **In a traditional application the developer writes the sequence; in an agent the model decides what happens next.** The four parts are a model that decides, tools it can call, state across steps, and **a loop with a stopping condition** — and the loop is the part people omit when describing one. **The answer that earns credit is knowing when not to:** if the steps are known in advance, write them, because a fixed pipeline is cheaper, testable and debuggable, and an agent rediscovering the same sequence is paying for flexibility it never uses.

d.title: Type 2, and the window function
d.caption: **The concrete reason Type 2 is the usual answer:** if a customer moves from London to Leeds, Type 1 silently restates last year's regional revenue, because every historical order now joins to Leeds. **And for the dedup, `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)` is what they are listening for**, because it makes “which copy survives” an explicit auditable decision rather than whatever the engine happened to keep — with a tiebreak after the timestamp, or the result is non-deterministic. d.title: Eleven layers, and the three nobody mentions
d.caption: **Almost every candidate lists monitoring and omits evaluation in CI, the per-user cost cap and feedback capture.** Without a golden set in CI, a prompt edit is an unreviewed deploy to production behaviour. Without a spend ceiling, an agent loop is an unbounded bill attached to a stranger's input. And a thumbs-down carrying the trace id is how the golden set grows from real failures rather than from imagination — which closes the loop between production and evaluation.

d.title: Does the flow need to loop or pause?
d.caption: **That one question decides it.** Retrieve-then-generate is a straight line and LCEL expresses it in a few lines. Retrieve, grade, maybe retry, maybe ask a human, then generate is a cycle with state — and expressing that as a chain means hand-rolling the loop, the state and the resumption, which is exactly what LangGraph is. **The answer that reads as experience adds the third option:** for a simple pipeline, neither — an SDK call and a vector client is less abstraction to debug.

d.title: At this difficulty the code is free - everything around it is the signal
d.caption: **Both of these are warm-ups, and both have one edge case that catches people.** Python's modulo is never negative, so `n % 2` classifies negatives correctly where C would give −1 and a `== 1` test would silently fail on every negative odd number. And `n < 2` is where most quick prime checks break — 0, 1 and negatives are not prime. **Say the edge cases before writing, state the complexity without being asked, and type-hint it**, because at this level that is the whole assessment.
